source: Schoenfeld (1981) Episodes and Executive Decisions in Mathematical Problem Solving (AERA paper)
finding: Founding paper of the control idea. A protocol is cut into episodes (Reading, Analysis, Exploration, Planning, Implementation, Verification, Transition). Managerial decisions are judged at the joints between episodes. Experts have vigilant managers; novices lack them.
numbers: Seven episode types; detailed protocols from two student pairs (1 to 3 semesters of college calculus), all undergraduates at a liberal arts college.
quote: Experts are shown to have rather "vigilant" managers, which strive for efficiency and accuracy.
limits: Speculative, evolving framework by the author's own words; the coding has a subjective part. Few detailed cases.
agent_relevance: S6 needs an explicit episode structure so code can see where a managerial decision is due.

source: Schoenfeld (1981) Episodes and Executive Decisions: three loci of managerial decisions
finding: A control decision is due at three places: (1) the junction between episodes when direction changes, (2) arrival of new information or a new idea, even mid-episode, (3) a run of tactical failures (implementation bogs down or exploration turns unstructured). Experts have monitors that call this review; novices often lack them.
numbers: Three loci named. The third (stall detection) is called hard to code and needs subjective judgment.
limits: The stall locus had 'no easy way' to be coded in 1981; an agent can code it (no change in K steps).
agent_relevance: Template for S6 trigger rules: fire on episode change, on a new idea, on a stall. The 'new idea surfaced' trigger is not in the schema yet.

source: Schoenfeld (1981) the circle-triangle wild goose chase protocol
finding: Two students were asked for the largest triangle inscribed in a circle. They guessed equilateral and spent the next 20 minutes computing its area. Nobody asked what the area would buy. Alternatives (calculus max-min, rectangle in a circle, varying the shape) surfaced and faded.
numbers: 20-minute session; at least three salvaging ideas dropped. Neither student could say afterward what the area would be used for.
quote: the students did not assess the potential utility of their planned actions
limits: One protocol, chosen as illustrative. Another paper by the same author says lone-student settings can induce odd behaviour (see a12).
agent_relevance: The failure was a missing assessment, not a wrong tactic. S6 should ask what an output will buy before long implementation.

source: Schoenfeld (1981) expert contrast: 'this is too complicated'
finding: In an expert protocol the solver interrupted a half-built solution with a complexity cue and stopped. Novices had no such termination rule once a wild goose chase began.
numbers: Qualitative; one expert case quoted.
quote: this is too complicated. I know the problem shouldn't be this hard.
limits: Anecdotal in this paper; the cue relies on prior knowledge of how hard the problem should be.
agent_relevance: Cheap trigger: derivation effort far above what the problem class normally needs.

source: Schoenfeld (1981) protocol 2: casual commitment steering over 60% of the time
finding: A second pair chose a symmetry assumption (which assumed what had to be proved) casually after one attempt failed. That choice steered more than 60% of the allotted time. They then turned from the failed attempt without asking what could be learned from it; the review was a once-over-lightly.
numbers: Decision at items 24 to 27; steered over 60% of the allotted time.
limits: One case. Shows two control failures: unjustified commitment, and abandoning with nothing salvaged.
agent_relevance: Abandoning needs a salvage step: record what the failed path established before dropping it.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) Expert and novice mathematical problem solving, final project report (ED218124): coding framework
finding: Final NSF report with the protocol-parsing framework. Coding is done on macroscopic episodes. Inter-coder reliability between the author and three student coders exceeded 85%. The report says the method gives one perspective and should be paired with tests and interviews.
numbers: Inter-coder reliability above 85%; three students code with the author.
limits: Reliability is agreement on episode parsing, not on the quality of the managerial decision, which stays subjective.
agent_relevance: Episode boundaries can be judged reliably, so code-detected boundaries are plausible.

source: Schoenfeld and Herrmann (1982) Problem perception and knowledge structure in expert and novice mathematical problem solvers
finding: Card-sort study. After a month-long problem-solving course, novices sorted problems more by deep structure and scored far higher on a test. A programming-course control group did not change.
numbers: 19 novices (11 in the problem-solving course, 8 in a programming control) plus 9 professors. Test mean 21 to 73 for the course group; 14 to 24 for control. Term x group F(1,17)=48.2, p<.001. Experts, non-coinciding pairs: surface .25 (3 of 12), deep .67 (8 of 12).
limits: Small N. Control group was paid; experimental group was enrolled in a course: different motivation. It is about problem perception, an input to control, not control itself.
agent_relevance: Teaching heuristics plus management can shift how problems are read; reading by deep structure precedes the managerial choice.

source: Schoenfeld (1983) Theoretical and pragmatic issues in the design of mathematical problem-solving instruction: seven of twelve
finding: Of twelve recorded student sessions in a 1981 experiment, seven were of the type 'read, then go on a wild goose chase'. Failures were traced to the control level: wild goose chases, unwarranted assumptions a monitor would have caught, and throwing away parts of a solution on abandoning.
numbers: 7 of 12 sessions (58%) were read-then-wild-goose-chase.
quote: read and then go on a wild goose chase
limits: N=12 sessions in one lab, college students. The 1985 book's wider counts were not read this session.
agent_relevance: A base rate: over half of weak attempts have no monitoring at all. A forced check at set budget points would catch many.

source: Schoenfeld (1983) why control failures are hidden and the three questions
finding: College freshmen see their minds as autonomous and just do what comes to mind. The costs of bad control are not immediate, so failure gets blamed elsewhere. Teachers show schema-based solutions, so students never see anyone think. Fix: the teacher asks three questions: What exactly are you doing? Why are you doing it? How does it help you?
numbers: Three questions; large- and small-group discussion framed by Vygotsky's zone of proximal development.
limits: A design proposal with classroom anecdotes; effect sizes sit in the 1985 book (not read).
agent_relevance: The three questions are a ready S6 check: state the action, say why, say what the output will be used for. If it cannot, stop.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving (book)
finding: Four-part framework: resources (knowledge), heuristics, control (monitoring and decisions) and belief systems. Control is the managerial layer that decides which resources and heuristics to use and when to quit.
numbers: Not read this session. No numbers recorded from it.
limits: Recalled, not opened. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Source of the resources/heuristics/control/beliefs split used by the schema row.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Students' beliefs about mathematics and their effects on performance: a questionnaire analysis
finding: Belief questionnaire of 230 students in grades 9 to 12. Almost half view math as mostly memorizing; three fourths think it helps a person think logically. In his earlier studies, over 90% of subjects solved a construction problem by trial and error, accepting or rejecting on purely empirical grounds.
numbers: 70 closed and 10 open questions; N=230. Over 90% empirical-only on Problem 3 (quoted from earlier studies).
limits: Self-report; mostly Math 10 geometry students; the 90% figure comes from other studies cited in the paper.
agent_relevance: Beliefs gate control: a solver who thinks the task is recall does not monitor. For the agent, prompt framing may play this role.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) Beyond the purely cognitive: metacognition and social cognition as driving forces in intellectual performance
finding: Lone-student think-aloud sessions on a body-volume and cell-volume estimation problem gave odd behaviour: very exact body-volume calculation and crude, unqualified cell-size guesses. About two dozen student pairs on the same problem never showed it. The author calls it pathology induced by the setting.
numbers: Perhaps two dozen pairs recorded; none showed the single-student behaviour.
quote: Not once did a pair of students demonstrate the kind of behavior I have just described.
limits: Anecdotal count. A warning that lone think-aloud can create the control failure it studies.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: observed poor control may be partly pressure on a lone solver. A second reader (pair format) exposes and may reduce it.

source: Garofalo and Lester (1985) Metacognition, cognitive monitoring, and mathematical performance (J. Research in Mathematics Education)
finding: Proposed a cognitive-metacognitive framework for mathematical performance with four phases: orientation, organization, execution, verification.
numbers: Article not opened. The four phases are confirmed only through the 1989 report that builds on it (a14).
limits: Not opened; the phase list is cross-checked only through the 1989 report.
agent_relevance: The four phases map roughly onto S1, S2/S3, S4/S5 and S8.

source: Lester, Garofalo and Kroll (1989) The role of metacognition in mathematical problem solving: a study of two grade seven classes (NSF final report)
finding: 12-week metacognition-based instruction in two grade 7 classes, about 3 days a week, by an investigator. Of the four categories, orientation (reading, understanding, judging difficulty before starting) mattered most. Instruction works best when long and inside normal lessons, not as a special unit. Scores rose on a 10-point test but there was no control class.
numbers: Regular class N=22: pretest mean 4.73, posttest 6.00. Advanced class N=34: 6.74 to 8.38 (max 10; OCR of the table order is imperfect). Advanced class showed a ceiling effect.
quote: the orientation category stands out as being the most important
limits: No control class (planned, then dropped). Gains cannot be separated from practice or maturation.
agent_relevance: Orientation first: a pre-attempt step judging what is asked and how hard it is has the highest value.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs alone, except in tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works well when reliable external feedback exists. Large-scale fine-tuning can enable it.
numbers: Three conclusions as in the abstract. Abstract and introduction read; not every section.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey of papers to 2024; later RL-trained reasoners may weaken the prompted-LLM claim.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3. A prompted 'check yourself' monitor is not a reliable trigger.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: With oracle labels, self-correction looks good; without them it hurts. Models change right answers to wrong ones more than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 standard: GSM8K 75.9, CommonSenseQA 75.8, HotpotQA 26.0. With oracle: 84.3, 89.7, 29.0. GPT-4 standard 95.5, 82.0, 49.0; with oracle 97.5, 85.5, 59.0. Intrinsic GPT-3.5 after round 2: GSM8K 74.7, CSQA 41.8, HotpotQA 25.0. Intrinsic GPT-4 round 2: 89.0, 80.0, 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 then 90.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2) and 2023 prompts; not RL-trained reasoners. Test sets about 100 to 200 items for some tasks.
agent_relevance: The S6 monitor must not be the model's own opinion of correctness; trigger from code.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format. A 52B model's P(True) on its own samples separates right from wrong. Models can be trained to predict P(IK), whether they know the answer, and this partly generalizes across tasks. Replacing an option with 'none of the above' hurts calibration.
numbers: 52B model; TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex HumanEval equally weighted in the self-evaluation summary. Calibration improves with size and from zero-shot to few-shot.
quote: as model size and capabilities increase, models improve at self-evaluation
limits: 2022 base-style models with token probabilities; sensitive to format. Verbalized confidence in chat models is a separate question.
agent_relevance: Token-level probabilities can feed a code-read trigger, unlike a verbal self-judgment.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive capabilities of LLMs: an exploration in mathematical problem solving
finding: GPT-4 labeled math questions with skill names that were clustered into coarse skills. At test time the model names the needed skill and gets exemplars of that skill. This lifts accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4-0613 gave about 500 unique skill names for 7,000 GSM8K items and 5,000 for 7,500 MATH items. MATH: +11.6% over CoT, +3.5% over Complex CoT and over topic-based exemplars. Program-aided prompts on 500 MATH items: +7.52% over PAL. About +4.0% over CoT with self-consistency.
limits: This is metacognitive knowledge (which skill is needed), not monitoring or control. Part of the gain is better exemplars.
agent_relevance: A cheap orientation step: name the skill before attacking; but the gain may be exemplar retrieval.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025, COLM) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners
finding: Four behaviors: verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining. Qwen-2.5-3B has them and improves under RL on Countdown; Llama-3.2-3B lacks them and plateaus. Priming Llama with these behaviors lets it match or beat Qwen.
numbers: Countdown after RL: Qwen about 60%, Llama about 30%. Controls: empty chain-of-thought or length-matched filler priming leaves Llama near base (30 to 35%). Priming with incorrect solutions that show the behaviors gave comparable gains to correct ones.
limits: 3B models; one main task (Countdown) with a transfer check; behaviors, not answer correctness, mattered here.
agent_relevance: Backtracking and verification are habits, not extra tokens. Supports a scaffold that triggers them.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models run many solution rounds even on trivial problems. Later rounds add little accuracy and little diversity. This is a missing stop monitor.
numbers: For '2 plus 3', 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one case had 13 solutions. In more than 92% of cases the first round already held the correct answer. QwQ-32B-Preview gave 3.5 solutions on average on the easiest set (ASDIV). Level 1 MATH outcome efficiency below 50%. Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with accuracy kept.
quote: In more than 92% of cases, the initial round of solutions produces the correct answer.
limits: Open models (QwQ, R1); the efficiency metrics are the authors' own; the fix needs weights.
agent_relevance: The mirror failure of the wild goose chase: too much checking. Trigger rules need a stop side (accept once verification passes).

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models abandon promising lines too early. Incorrect answers show more thought switches and more tokens. Over 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought. A decoding penalty on switch tokens (TIP) raises accuracy.
numbers: Underthinking score (higher is more wasted tokens): MATH500-Hard QwQ-32B-Preview acc 84.3, UT 58.2; R1-Preview 83.6, 61.5; R1-671B 92.5, 65.4. TIP Pass@1 over 32 samples: AIME2024 QwQ 38.3 to 44.1; R1-Distill-32B 61.4 to 64.1; MATH500-Hard QwQ 83.1 to 83.7; GPQA Diamond QwQ 57.6 to 59.1.
quote: over 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought
limits: Gains small on easy sets; AIME is 30 problems (plus 60 earlier ones); penalty settings tuned on AIME 2022/23.
agent_relevance: Premature abandoning is measurable. S6 should abandon on a trigger, not at every 'alternatively'.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: After a failed trial the agent writes a short verbal reflection from the environment's signal and stores it for the next trial. It works where the signal is reliable.
numbers: AlfWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks within 12 trials. HumanEval pass@1: 91.0 against GPT-4 80.1. A simple heuristic detects hallucination and inefficient planning to trigger reflection.
limits: Needs a binary success signal or unit tests. The paper warns that flaky self-written tests can pass wrong code. Huang et al. show such gains vanish without an oracle.
agent_relevance: Reflection triggered by a real failure signal, then carried to the next attempt: matches S5/S6.

source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: a new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry
finding: Introduced metacognition as knowledge about, and regulation of, one's own cognition, including monitoring experiences and strategy choice.
numbers: Not opened this session.
limits: Recalled, not read. Do not cite figures from this line.
agent_relevance: Source of the knowledge/regulation split used by Garofalo and Lester and by Schoenfeld.

source: Lester (1994) Musings about mathematical problem-solving research: 1970-1994
finding: A review expected to judge the metacognition work of the 1980s promising but thin on training effects.
numbers: Not opened this session.
limits: Recalled, unverified. Check before use.
agent_relevance: Reminder to look for failed training replications (angle B).

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors: Qwen shifts from explicit to implicit checking
finding: Under RL, Qwen shows a step change near step 30 with longer responses and better accuracy. Later its verification moves from explicit statements ('8*35 is 280 which is too high') to implicit checking by trying solutions in turn.
numbers: Countdown: Qwen about 60% vs Llama about 30% at the end of training. Primed with empty chain-of-thought, Qwen stopped exploring the behaviors (training with empty CoT hurt).
limits: 3B models, one task. Counting verbal check phrases can undercount implicit checking.
agent_relevance: A detector that counts words like 'wait' or 'check' as monitoring may miss implicit monitoring; trigger rules should use code-visible events.

source: Huang et al. (2024) why intrinsic self-correction fails: option bias and confidence
finding: On CommonSenseQA the self-correction prompt pushes models to change answers because wrong options look partly relevant; GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo keep their first answers more, possibly from higher confidence.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 after one self-correction round (oracle stop not used). GSM8K barely moved because 74.7% of answers were kept.
limits: Prompt wording matters: the authors tried several self-correction prompts and all lowered performance, but only on 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A 'are you sure' trigger is itself a source of damage; require an observed failure before reopening an answer.
